paper.disclaimer: Method note, not advice. Not a valuation report.
paper.lead: Method D is the default way we value directly held Swiss residential property. It produces a range, not a price, and it names its index and its date. This note explains the inputs, works an example, and states what the method does not do.
paper.s1_h: Why a range, not a number
paper.s1_p: A listed security has a price: the last trade on an exchange, with a time stamp. A flat does not. The only honest output of a model fed by an index and adjustment factors is a central estimate with a band around it. We show the band. A single number would imply a precision the inputs do not carry.
paper.s2_p: Four inputs. The purchase price and its date. The cantonal or municipal house-price index for the relevant segment, which moves the purchase price to today. An age factor for the building. A condition factor for the unit, set from a short checklist you fill in. The index does the heavy lifting; the factors are deliberately coarse, because a fine-grained factor would be false precision.
paper.s3_p: A Zurich apartment bought in 2016 for CHF 1,210,000. The relevant index has risen 19 percent to the latest reading, dated 12 September 2026, which gives CHF 1,440,000. An age factor of 0.99 and a condition factor of 0.99 bring the central estimate to about CHF 1,412,000. We report a band of plus or minus five percent around it, so CHF 1,412,000 to 1,548,000. The index source and its date sit beside the number in the app.
paper.s4_p: It is not a valuation report and it is not advice. It does not replace a chartered surveyor, it does not account for micro-location within a building, and it does not reflect a formal appraisal. It exists so that a large illiquid line in your net worth is not a blank, and so that the number you do show carries a method, a source and a date.
paper.s5_p: Every property line in the app shows the index name, the index date and the factors used. If the index date ages past a threshold, the value is flagged as stale rather than silently carried forward. That is the same rule the market tiles follow, and it is the rule that makes the number usable rather than decorative.

paper2.title: What the private investor rule does not cover
paper2.lead: In Switzerland a private investor pays no tax on capital gains from securities. That is the headline. This note sets out where the rule starts to bend, and why the judgment for your own situation belongs to a tax adviser, not to software.
paper2.s1_p: Under Art. 16(3) of the federal direct tax law, capital gains on privately held movable assets are not taxed. Shares, funds, bonds and crypto held as private wealth can be sold at a profit and the gain stays out of taxable income at federal level and in most cantons. Only the income the asset produces, dividends and interest, is taxed as it is paid. The gain itself is not the trigger.
paper2.s2_h: Where it stops: the professional dealer
paper2.s2_p: The same article exempts the gain only for a private investor. If the tax office reclassifies you as a professional securities dealer, the gains become taxable income and the whole exemption falls away. The Federal Tax Administration set out the test in Circular No. 36 of 27 July 2012. It looks at a bundle of habits rather than one number, and an investor who trips several of them can lose the exemption even when each habit looks modest on its own.
paper2.s3_p: Circular No. 36 weighs several factors. A holding period under six months, a trading volume above five times the portfolio at the start of the year, gains that make up more than half of net income, leverage, and heavy use of derivatives all count against you. A clean private investor tends to hold longer than six months, trades well under five times the portfolio, keeps gains below half of income, and does not run the book on borrowed money. These are the safe-harbour markers the Administration describes, not a formula that guarantees a result.
paper2.s4_h: Two cases the rule never covers
paper2.s4_p: Two things sit outside the exemption no matter how patient you are. A gain on Swiss real estate is always taxed, through the cantonal real-estate gains tax (Grundstückgewinnsteuer), which is separate from income tax and has its own rates and holding-period relief. Employee shares and options carry their own rules, and a discount at grant can be taxed as income long before you sell. And the assets themselves still feed the annual wealth tax, which is levied on the holding whether or not it ever produces a gain.
paper2.s5_p: The app can show you a realized gain and its holding period. It can flag a position held under six months, or a year where disposals ran high against the portfolio. What it cannot do is decide whether your pattern of trades crosses into professional dealing, because that is a judgment on your whole situation, not a lookup. That call belongs to your tax adviser. We mark the flag and hand you the evidence.
paper2.disclaimer: Tax information, not tax advice. The classification of a private investor is a judgment for your adviser. See Art. 16(3) DBG and FTA Circular No. 36 of 27 July 2012.

edu.concept.inflation.name: Inflation
edu.concept.inflation.note: Inflation is the rate at which the general price level rises, so a given amount of cash buys less over time. Real return is the return after inflation, and it can be negative even when the nominal value is unchanged.
edu.concept.diversification.name: Diversification
edu.concept.diversification.note: Diversification spreads exposure across assets whose prices do not move in lockstep. It reduces the effect of any single holding, but it does not remove market risk and it cannot guarantee a result.
edu.concept.risk_return.name: Risk and return
edu.concept.risk_return.note: Risk and return are related: assets that can move more in the short term are generally expected to offer more over the long term, which also means a larger chance of loss. Expected is not promised.
edu.concept.liquidity.name: Liquidity
edu.concept.liquidity.note: Liquidity is how quickly and cheaply an asset can be turned into cash at a fair price. Cash is the most liquid; property, private stakes and collectibles can take time to convert and may trade at a discount if converted quickly.
edu.concept.volatility.name: Volatility
edu.concept.volatility.note: Volatility is how much a price moves around its average. Higher volatility means a wider range of outcomes over a given period, in both directions.
edu.cash.note: Cash is the most liquid holding and keeps its nominal value, so it is the ballast for near-term needs. Its main trade-off is inflation: over long periods, cash that earns little can lose purchasing power.
edu.bonds.note: Bonds are loans to a government or a company that pay interest and return principal at maturity. They can be ballast for a portfolio, but their prices fall when interest rates rise and a borrower can default.
edu.equity.note: Equity is part-ownership of a company, sharing in its profits and its risks. Over long periods equity has tended to grow, but it can fall sharply in a correction and can take years to recover.
edu.metals.note: Gold and other precious metals are stores of value that often hold up when inflation or uncertainty rises. They pay no income or dividend, so their return comes only from a change in price.
edu.realestate.note: Real estate is property held directly or through funds. It can earn rent and often tracks inflation over time, but it is illiquid: selling takes time and costs, and values can fall in a downturn.
edu.private.note: Private investments are stakes in unlisted companies or funds. They are illiquid and are committed for years, the value is based on periodic appraisals rather than a daily market, and they carry higher risk than listed assets.
edu.crypto.note: Crypto assets are digital holdings that trade around the clock and can move very sharply. Their value rests on adoption and sentiment rather than on earnings or interest, so they are highly volatile and can lose most of their value.
edu.collectibles.note: Collectibles such as art and watches are valued by the market for that object, not by a stream of income. They are illiquid, costly to insure and store, and their prices can be sensitive to fashion.
edu.vehicles.note: Vehicles are used assets that generally lose value over time. They are illiquid and usually count as consumption rather than investment, kept in the ledger for a complete net worth.
edu.context.level: {symbol} is shown at its last stored source with its date. No prior reading is stored, so no change is shown.
edu.context.steady: {symbol} is close to its previous reading, so the one-step change is small.
edu.context.up.steady: {symbol} is modestly higher than its previous reading. A single move of this size says little about what comes next.
edu.context.up.modest: {symbol} has risen versus its previous reading. Larger moves raise the volatility of a portfolio that holds it, in both directions.
edu.context.up.notable: {symbol} has risen sharply versus its previous reading. A concentrated position in it would have grown, and so would its share of a portfolio, which is what drift measures.
edu.context.up.sharp: {symbol} has risen very sharply versus its previous reading. Moves of this size show how fast a level can change, and they cut both ways.
edu.context.down.steady: {symbol} is modestly lower than its previous reading. A single move of this size says little about what comes next.
edu.context.down.modest: {symbol} has fallen versus its previous reading. Larger moves raise the volatility of a portfolio that holds it, in both directions.
edu.context.down.notable: {symbol} has fallen sharply versus its previous reading. A concentrated position in it would have shrunk, and so would its share of a portfolio, which is what drift measures.
edu.context.down.sharp: {symbol} has fallen very sharply versus its previous reading. Moves of this size show how fast a level can change, and they cut both ways.
edu.context.vix.calm: The VIX is in a calm band, below 15, meaning the options market prices a quiet near term. A calm reading is a description of today, not a prediction.
edu.context.vix.normal: The VIX is in its long-run normal band, 15 to 20, a middle reading on the options market's view of near-term movement.
edu.context.vix.cautious: The VIX is in a cautious band, 20 to 30, meaning the options market prices more movement than usual. A higher reading means a wider range of outcomes, not a direction.
edu.context.vix.stressed: The VIX is in a stressed band, above 30, meaning the options market prices a turbulent near term. Stress subsides over time, but the timing is not knowable from the level alone.
insights.education.title: Education
insights.education.sub: Plain-language notes on what each asset class is and does, and a descriptive read of today's levels. Sourced, dated, governance screened, never advice.
checkin.title: Did your life circumstance change?
checkin.sub: A life event usually changes what your money needs to do: how much cash you can reach, how long it can stay invested, and how much a fall can be carried. Mark any that apply and see the general consequences. Information about the event, not advice about your holdings.
checkin.pick.lead: Choose the event that happened. The consequences are general and sourced; the answer is dated and kept with your account so a later session can come back to it.
checkin.result.empty: Pick an event above to see its usual consequences.
checkin.note.notadvice: General information about a life event, not investment advice.
checkin.new_baby.liquidity: A new baby usually raises regular costs and adds one-off expenses, so the cash buffer that covers a few months of spending tends to need to be larger.
checkin.new_baby.horizon: Childcare and education costs arrive over many years, which shortens the span before some money is needed and lengthens it for money set aside for later.
checkin.new_baby.risk: With less slack in the monthly budget, a market fall is harder to ride out, because selling to meet costs can lock in a loss.
checkin.house_purchase.liquidity: Buying a home concentrates a large share of net worth in one illiquid asset, so day-to-day cash and a reserve for repairs matter more.
checkin.house_purchase.horizon: A mortgage is a long, fixed commitment, so the horizon for the money tied to the property is measured in years, not months.
checkin.house_purchase.risk: A single large, illiquid holding raises concentration: a local property downturn touches the whole net worth at once.
checkin.divorce.liquidity: A separation often splits accounts and assets and adds legal costs, so cash that can be reached quickly matters more.
checkin.divorce.horizon: Splitting a household can reorder long-term plans, so some goals move further out while others come sooner.
checkin.divorce.risk: Two households cost more than one, which leaves less room to absorb a market fall without selling.
checkin.unemployment.liquidity: Job loss removes regular income, so an emergency buffer covering several months of costs is the first thing that matters.
checkin.unemployment.horizon: With no incoming salary, money that was set aside for the long term may be needed sooner, which shortens its horizon.
checkin.unemployment.risk: Depending on investments to cover living costs during a gap means a fall can force sales at the worst time.
checkin.inheritance.liquidity: An inheritance usually adds cash or assets at once, which can raise both the buffer and the amount that needs a plan.
checkin.inheritance.horizon: Sudden wealth can be invested for a long horizon, and the decision does not have to be immediate.
checkin.inheritance.risk: A large single addition can shift the mix of assets, which is what concentration and drift measure.
checkin.health.liquidity: A health event can bring unplanned costs and time away from work, so easily reachable cash matters more.
checkin.health.horizon: If income or working life changes, the span before money is needed can shorten, so some goals move closer.
checkin.health.risk: With less certainty about future income, a fall in investments is harder to wait out.
profile.quiz.lead: Seven short questions. Your answers map to a suggested style by an open rule, shown below. Clear the answers to choose a style by hand.
profile.q.horizon: How long before you would need a large part of this money?
profile.q.stage: Which stage of life are you closest to?
profile.q.dependents: Who depends on this money besides you?
profile.o.dependents.0: Children or others who rely on it
profile.q.emergency: How many months of expenses could you cover from cash if income stopped?
profile.q.property: Do you plan to buy property with this money soon?
profile.q.drop: If your portfolio fell 25% in a year, what would you do?
profile.reason.base: Answering horizon and reaction to a fall gives a base score of {base} out of 6.
profile.reason.capacity: Capacity, read from horizon, income stability, stage of life and dependents, scores {capacity} out of 3 and sets a ceiling of twice that.
profile.reason.liquidity: Liquidity, read from the emergency buffer and any near-term property plan, scores {liquidity} out of 3 and caps the result at twice that.
profile.reason.override.capacity: A capacity signal set the ceiling below the base score, so the style follows the lower, more affordable figure. This is education about how the answers usually map, not a suitability assessment.
profile.reason.override.liquidity: A liquidity signal set the ceiling below the base score, so the style follows the more liquid figure. This is education about how the answers usually map, not a suitability assessment.
profile.rule: Open rule: the base score is horizon plus reaction to a fall (0 to 6). Capacity and liquidity each set a ceiling (0 to 6); the lower ceiling binds, and the fit is the lower of the base and that ceiling. A short horizon or a thin buffer is not lifted by a high willingness to take risk. An open rule, not a black box.
profile.note.notadvice: How these answers usually map to an illustrative style. General information, not investment advice, and not a suitability assessment.
profile.reason.withheld: The reasoning was withheld by the governance gate.
edu.valuation.lead: A descriptive read of the equity multiple versus the same index's own long-run reference, each from a named, dated source. It describes a level, not a forecast, and never a call.
edu.val.empty: No sourced valuation reading is available yet. Valuation appears once a dated row is added to the table.
edu.context.valuation.cheap: {symbol} is shown at a valuation below its own long-run reference ({pe} against {reference_pe}, source and date cited). A lower starting multiple has historically accompanied higher long-run returns, but this describes the level, it is not a forecast.
edu.context.valuation.fair: {symbol} is shown at a valuation close to its own long-run reference ({pe} against {reference_pe}, source and date cited). A multiple near its own history is a middle reading; it says nothing on its own about what comes next.
edu.context.valuation.elevated: {symbol} is shown at an elevated valuation versus its own history ({pe} against {reference_pe}, source and date cited). Higher starting multiples have historically accompanied lower long-run returns and deeper drawdowns, but this is a description, not a prediction.
edu.context.valuation.expensive: {symbol} is shown at a valuation well above its own long-run reference ({pe} against {reference_pe}, source and date cited). Very high starting multiples have historically accompanied lower long-run returns and deeper drawdowns, and they can persist for a long time; this is a description, not a forecast.
